profiles.meeting_scenario: An ML research troubleshooting meeting between a postdoc and a research engineer working on reproducing the CLIP paper's training behavior for image classification. Over the last week, their internal reimplementation on Fashion-MNIST has shown an unstable pattern: runs with CLIP regularization sometimes look smoother during training but fail to improve robustness in the final report, and in some seeds the regularizer appears to dominate optimization much earlier than expected. The meeting is scheduled because they need to diagnose why their reproduction diverges from the paper's reported behavior before a lab-wide update. The agenda is to compare what each person has observed, identify the most likely root cause of the discrepancy, and agree on a minimal fix to test today. The expected outcome is a concrete troubleshooting plan for the next run, including what to change, what logs to inspect, and what they will consider a successful fix.

members.name: Dr. Mira Chen
members.expertise: robust machine learning, variational regularization, empirical analysis of stability methods
members.background: Mira recently joined the lab from a theory-heavy group where she worked on stability guarantees and usually evaluates methods by comparing training dynamics across controlled replications of papers.
members.private_state: She wants the reproduction to be defensible in the upcoming group review and is quietly worried that the current discrepancy may come from an implementation detail that would make their negative result look careless rather than substantive.
hidden_assumptions: When discussing the 'CLIP penalty strength,' the meaningful quantity is the per-minibatch coefficient exactly as inserted into the training loss each optimization step.
A 'stable' reproduction means the regularizer produces comparable training dynamics and smoothness behavior throughout training, not just a similar endpoint metric.
Saying they should 'match the paper setup' includes matching the effective optimization schedule under the original batch-size convention, even if their hardware forces different batching.
If someone says they already 'checked robustness,' that normally refers to the evaluation protocol used in the paper's final table rather than an intermediate stress test.

members.name: Arjun Patel
members.expertise: PyTorch training systems, experiment orchestration, reproducibility infrastructure
members.background: Arjun maintains the lab's training codebase and adapted the CLIP method into an existing image-classification pipeline that automatically handles gradient accumulation, logging, and robustness sweeps.
members.private_state: He wants to resolve the issue without rewriting the training loop and is quietly hoping the problem is just a calibration mismatch in evaluation or logging rather than a deeper flaw in the implementation.
hidden_assumptions: When discussing the 'CLIP penalty strength,' the meaningful quantity is the effective coefficient per optimizer update after gradient accumulation, because that is what determines parameter movement.
A 'stable' reproduction means the final trained model is less sensitive on the lab's robustness check, even if the training curve shape differs from the paper.

Saying they should 'match the paper setup' means preserving the nominal hyperparameters from the config file, while letting the standard pipeline handle batch accumulation and normalization details automatically.
If someone says they already 'checked robustness,' that can naturally refer to the lab's fast FGSM sweep used for troubleshooting before running the full reporting protocol.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about keeping 'the same lambda' for the CLIP regularizer.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the scalar lambda multiplying the CLIP term in each minibatch loss before backprop, so changing effective batch handling changes the practical regularization regime unless compensated.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the effective regularization weight per optimizer step after the pipeline's gradient accumulation, so the config can keep the same nominal lambda while the framework averages losses internally.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are experienced enough that 'same lambda' sounds like an unambiguous low-level implementation detail, and each assumes the other is using the standard meaning from their own workflow.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to whether the run 'improves robustness.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means improvement on the paper-aligned final evaluation, especially consistency with the reported clean/perturbed tradeoff at the end of training.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means improvement on the lab's quick FGSM-based diagnostic sweep run during development to see whether sensitivity drops at all.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In troubleshooting meetings, 'robustness' is often used as shorthand because everyone expects a related family of stress tests, and both measures plausibly move in the same direction, so the distinction feels too minor to spell out.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both compare the current CLIP run against 'the baseline run from last Thursday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the 2-layer Fashion-MNIST baseline trained with the paper-faithful small architecture that she used for curve comparisons in her notes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the standard lab baseline launched last Thursday in the shared dashboard, which used the same dataset but the pipeline's wider default backbone.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There really was a baseline run on Thursday in both of their workflows, and because both were on Fashion-MNIST and temporally close, each assumes there is only one salient reference.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to 'patch the training loop' before rerunning.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a narrow scientific fix: adjust only the CLIP-term scaling/logging path so the reproduction remains directly comparable to the paper.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a broader infrastructure patch: update the shared trainer's loss normalization and robustness-hook defaults so future runs are consistent across methods.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see the patch as a practical next step and use the same phrase, but one is thinking about experimental validity while the other is thinking about codebase consistency; neither expects that boundary to be contentious in a short troubleshooting call.

turns.inner_thought: The pattern still bothers me. In the paper-aligned sense, CLIP should not just make the curves look nicer early; it should also show the expected end-of-training clean/perturbed tradeoff in the final evaluation. If we go into group review with 'it looks smoother but doesn't improve robustness,' I need to be sure we're not missing some mundane implementation detail that would make the negative result look sloppy.
